name: Science, religion, and the question of design
description: The argument over geology, deep time, development and design, and the literature it made. Lyell's Principles of Geology (vols. 1–3, 1830–33) and the anonymous Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (1844) prepare Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) and Descent of Man (1871), and Tennyson's "Nature red to tooth and claw" in In Memoriam (1849/50) gives the argument its lyric phrase. Its British literary endpoints are the development hypothesis of Robert Browning's Bishop Blougram's Apology (in Men and Women, 1855), the anthropological romance of Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872) and the evolution-and-degeneration fiction of the 1890s; in America the same argument is carried in the reviews, the lecture and the heredity novel of the 1870s and 1880s.

name: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience
description: The felt loss of belief and the attempts to rebuild religion without the dogma. Essays and Reviews (1860) and the Privy Council's judgment in the controversy in 1864, the Broad Church theology of Maurice, Jowett and Kingsley, and the anonymously published Ecce Homo (1866) define the positions; the word "agnostic" is coined in the later 1860s and Tyndall's Belfast address of 1868 states the scientific claim. In literature the theme is the "doubt" of In Memoriam (1849/50), Arnold's "Dover Beach" (printed 1867), Clough's ironic verse narratives of the 1850s, and the religion of humanity of the positivist and ethical societies.

name: Bereavement, immortality, and the argument from grief
description: Grief treated as both fact and evidence. Tennyson's In Memoriam A.H.H. (privately printed 1849, title page 1850), written on the death of Arthur Hallam, makes the long mourning-sequence the age's central form; Arnold's "Thyrsis" (1866) mourns a friend in pastoral terms; America's parallel is Whitman's Lincoln elegies of 1865. The theme also covers the culture of mourning — the funeral, the monument, the photograph, the spiritualist's seance — that the period's domestic fiction repeatedly registers.

name: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman
description: The argument over the legal being, education, property and franchise of women, and its fiction. The Married Women's Property Act (1882) and the campaign over the Contagious Diseases Acts in the 1870s and 1880s give it a legal shape; the tracts and review essays on women's franchise, education and paid labour of the 1850s to the 1870s are its debates, and Mill's The Subjection of Women (1869) its most quoted statement. Its literature runs from the marriage plots of Jane Eyre (1847) through Eliot's Middlemarch (serialised 1871–72) to Gissing's The Odd Women (1893), Allen's The Woman Who Did (1895) and Chopin's The Awakening (1899).

name: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations
description: The moral and narrative problem of industrial wage labour. Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845) names the division, Gaskell's Mary Barton (1848) and North and South (1855) give it a Manchester plot, Hard Times (serialised 1854) satirises its political economy, and at the century's close Gissing's The Nether World (1889) and Moore's Esther Waters (1894) return to it in naturalist terms.

name: The metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital
description: London as a vast, unreadable modern city. Bleak House (serialised 1852–53) makes the fog, the court and the slum a single system; the documented survey of the capital — Mayhew's enquiries of the early 1850s and Booth's enquiry begun in the late 1880s — the West End and East End essay, the impressionist walking tour of the 1880s and 1890s and the poem of the crowd complete the theme. Its American twin is T21.

name: Empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole
description: The empire as subject, audience and vocabulary. Indian Mutiny and Crown rule after 1857–58, the Crimean campaign, the Sudan and the South African war of 1899 supply the material; the boy's imperial romance (Haggard's King Solomon's Mines, 1885), Kipling's verse and tales of the 1880s and 1890s, and the "jingo" temper of the later 1890s and of the Jubilees of 1887 and 1897 give it its public language, with Conrad's and Kipling's fiction the most quoted literary answers to it.

name: Education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self
description: The formation of mind as a social and moral question. Newman's The Idea of a University (1852, enlarged 1873), Arnold's Culture and Anarchy (1869) and his lecture "On the Study of Celtic Literature" (1867) give it the theory; the public-school story (Hughes's Tom Brown's School Days, 1857), the school-board and pupil-teacher novel, and the autodidact's memoir give it the institution; the education of the girl — from Jane Eyre (1847) to the college heroine of the 1890s — is its most argued branch.

name: Madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will
description: Insanity as plot, as medicine and as metaphor. Sensation fiction makes the private asylum a machine of dispossession in The Woman in White (1859–60), Lady Audley's Secret (1862) and Armadale (1866); the "monomania" and the hereditary taint pass into the naturalist case history (Norris's McTeague, 1899) and into the diagnosis of the self-destructive will in The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890). Behind the fiction are the Lunacy Acts of the 1840s, the rapidly growing county and private asylum, and the new clinical psychology of the diagnosis.

name: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination
description: Finance as a moral and narrative force. Dickens's Little Dorrit (serialised 1855–57) makes the joint-stock mania and its official "Circumlocution" a single system; The Egoist (1879) treats money as a property of the will; Trollope's Phineas Finn (1867) and its sequel put the share and the election on the same page; and the commercial panic and the ruin of the speculator are stock plots of Gissing's New Grub Street (1891) and of the finance novel of the 1890s.

name: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income
description: The rentier, the "lady of means" and moneyed idleness as a social type and a moral problem. The unearned income of the country house and the London season is the material of Trollope's Phineas Finn (1867) and of Meredith's The Egoist (1879), and the "idle class" of the agricultural novel; the American branch is the millionaire comedy of the 1870s and 1880s — Twain and Warner's The Gilded Age (1873) — and the "conspicuous consumption" of Thorstein Veblen's analysis (1899).

name: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist
description: The quarrel between the demands of art and the demands of living, conducted in the novel and the memoir of the artist. Its instances are the professional writer's dilemma of the 1860s, Pater's "hard, gemlike flame" in the Renaissance studies of 1873 and the artist-hero of Marius the Epicurean (1885), Morris's artist-craftsman of the 1870s and 1880s, and Gissing's New Grub Street (1891) as the commercial case of the same quarrel.

name: Self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict
description: Suicide as plot, as disease and as public question. The drownings, poisonings and falls of sensation and realist fiction, the ruin endings of Hardy and of the naturalists, and the self-willed destruction of The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890) give it its narrative forms; its social documents are the coroner's inquest and its verdict and the statistical discussion of suicide in the 1860s and 1880s. The American instance is Chopin's ambiguous walk into the sea in The Awakening (1899).

name: Sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil
description: Regulated sex, prostitution, venereal disease and the sexual double standard as public subjects. The Contagious Diseases Acts and their repeal (the protest literature of 1885–86) create the "social evil" debate; the "fallen woman" novel of the 1850s and 1860s and its late-century counterparts — Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), the New Woman fiction of the 1890s and the "white slavery" panic of the same decade — give it its fiction.

name: The machinery of print: the serial, the magazine, and the book trade
description: The period's own publishing apparatus as a subject of its writing. The monthly part and the weekly serial, the three-volume library novel and the railway bookstall, Household Words (1850–59) and All the Year Round (1859–69), the American monthlies from The Atlantic (1857) onward, and the "conditions of letters" novel of the 1890s make the trade itself a theme.

name: Childhood, the child labourer, and the sentimental child
description: The child as economic unit, as sentimental icon and as narrator. The child-labour commission evidence of the 1840s, the "factory child" of Mary Barton (1848) and Hard Times (1854), the sentimental and holy child of The Water-Babies (1863) and the fairy tale, and the boy narrators of the 1870s to 1890s make the theme one of the period's most persistent.

name: The American wilderness and the myth of the forest
description: The forest as a moral and national space, after Cooper's eighteenth-century "Leather-Stocking" of the 1820s. In Transcendentalist writing it becomes a system of symbols — Emerson's Nature (1836) and Thoreau's Walden (1854) — and in Melville's and Hawthorne's romance it is a scene of guilt and of terror; the later regionalists keep it as a landscape of memory. The survey and the settlement, not the sublimity alone, govern the American writing.

name: Democracy, individualism, and the American experiment
description: The relation of the individual to the democratic whole. Emerson's "Self-Reliance" (1844) and "The American Scholar" (1837) state the ideal; Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855) makes it poetic; the anti-democratic diagnosis runs from Melville's The Confidence-Man (1857) to Twain's political tales of the 1870s to 1890s. Tocqueville's Democracy in America (French 1835–40; the English translation from the later 1830s) is the period's standard description of the same problem.

name: Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction
description: The literature of American slavery, its destruction and its aftermath. Douglass's Narrative (1845), Jacobs's Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861) and the anti-slavery lecture platform give the testimony; Stowe's A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1853) and her later novels make the argument a popular one; after the war, Tourgée's A Fool's Errand (1879), Dunbar's poems and prose of the 1890s, Chesnutt's tales of the colour line of 1899 to 1901 and Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884/85) register emancipation's incompleteness.

name: The closing of the American frontier
description: The settlement line, the "empty" West and its declared end. The emigrant generation wrote the trail narrative in the 1840s — Parkman's prairie and Rocky Mountain sketches of 1849 — and after the census declaration of a settled frontier line in the early 1890s, the essay "The Significance of the Frontier in American History", delivered in 1893, made the closing an official theme. Frederick Jackson Turner's "frontier thesis" is the interpretation of American character built on it, and the regionalist and imperial writing of the 1890s are its literary consequences.

name: The American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis
description: The great city, its wealth and its mechanisms, as the new American scene. Howells's A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890) puts the strike, the newspaper and the fashionable quarter on one page; Crane's Maggie (1893) makes the slum and the machine a destiny; and the skyscraper city of the 1890s — its elevated railway, its electric light and its crowded ward — is the setting of the naturalists and of the Chicago Bohemia of the later decade.

name: Innocence, experience, and the lost American Eden
description: The American theme of an innocence discovered to be knowledge. It runs from the "education" of Twain's and James's innocents — James's Daisy Miller (1878–79) and The Portrait of a Lady (1881) — to the lost country of the post-bellum regional tale and to the innocence of the child before the fact of race in Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884/85).

name: Regional identity and the American sectional character
description: The belief that a "section" makes a character, and the literature that markets it. Harte's California stories of the late 1860s, Jewett's Maine coastal village in The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896), the New England village tales of the 1880s and 1890s, Harris's Georgia of the 1880s and Cable's Louisiana all define the American self by a scene, a speech and a type, and the sectional "survey" of the 1880s gives the theme its taxonomy.

name: Industrial wealth, accumulation, and the gospel of accumulation
description: The American millionaire, the trust and the moral justification of wealth. Carnegie's essay "The Gospel of Wealth" (1889) and the "Gilded Age" — the name given to the 1870s by Twain and Warner's novel of that title (1873) — provide the vocabulary; Howells's The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885) makes the paint manufacturer a tragicomic figure, and the "money versus labour" quarrel of the 1890s is the naturalists' subject.

name: Race, voice, and the dialect of freedom
description: American writing in or about black speech after emancipation. Harris's dialect tales, published as Uncle Remus, His Songs and His Sayings (1880), and the recited dialect verse of the 1880s and 1890s, of which Dunbar is the standard example, make dialect a national medium; Chesnutt's The Conjure Woman (1899) uses the same frame to interrogate it, and the race-and-lineage plots of American fiction of the 1890s give the theme its tragic form.

name: The machine age, speed, and technical modernity
description: The machine, railway, telegraph, telephone, electric light and camera as literary subjects. The railway and the accident are plots from the 1840s onward — the train in The Woman in White (1859–60) and the railway collision of the sensation and later sensation drama; the telephone and the phonograph, the skyscraper's lift and the electric city are the equipment of the 1890s; in fiction the machine is the figure of determinism in Norris and of the future in Bellamy (1888) and Wells.

name: Bohemia, the professional writer, and the Grub Street market
description: Literature as a trade and the writer as a paid professional. Borrow's Lavengro (1851) makes the learned vagabond a figure of letters, the "Grub Street" novel of the 1890s — Gissing's New Grub Street (1891) is its classic and Du Maurier's Trilby (1894) its Bohemian parody — records the market, and the little magazine, the recital and the lecture circuit, together with the American authors' fight over international copyright in the 1880s and 1890s, make the trade itself the theme.
